_comment: Measured quality floors. A change that drops below any of these fails the guard.
These are FLOORS, not targets. Raise them when a change earns it, deliberately,
in the same commit that earns it. Lowering one is a decision that must be argued
in a commit message, never a convenience to make a build pass.
THE HELD-OUT SPLIT CHANGED, so numbers before 2026-09-01 are NOT comparable.
mechanism/appliesTo used to be held out and are now indexed; observation notes
and prediction reasoning replaced them. See src/lib/cairn/evalset.ts. The old
split scored 0.895 and the new one scores 0.836 on the same retriever -- the
new split is harder because it is people describing an encounter in their own
words rather than the author's own explanation of the finding.
Two suites are tracked because they measure different query distributions and
have disagreed. Held-out queries are plentiful; agent queries are real tool
stderr, representative but few. A change that improves one and damages the
other is a trade to be made consciously, which is why both appear here.

heldOut._source: npm run cairn:eval — observation notes and prediction reasoning, never indexed
_note: REBASED. The former split (mechanism/appliesTo) is now indexed and appears in
the report as an in-sample tripwire scoring 1.000, which measures nothing.
Indexing those fields was measured on THIS split, held out both before and
after, which is the only comparison that means anything:
before  P@1 0.821  P@5 0.910  MRR 0.864  delivery 0.851
after   P@1 0.836  P@5 0.910  MRR 0.876  delivery 0.851
One case of 67. Worth having and far short of what the old split implied,
for the reason recorded in evalset.ts: a field cannot be indexed and held
out, so 1.000 on the old split was the measurement collapsing, not accuracy.
The weak-field damp is a real trade and was chosen on the machine suite.
At damp >= 0.8 held-out is 0.851 and machine stderr drops to 7/8; at <= 0.7
held-out is 0.836, P@5 is better (0.910 vs 0.896) and machine holds 8/8.
Machine stderr is what production actually receives, so it wins.
LOWERED 0.86 -> 0.84 and MRR 0.87 -> 0.88 on 2026-09-01 when cairn-0032 was
added. A new finding competes with the existing ones, so P@1 moving is
expected and is not a regression in the ranker: 0.864 -> 0.851 is one case
of 67. The floor moves because the corpus changed, which is the one reason
it is allowed to.
LOWERED AGAIN 0.84 -> 0.83 (MRR 0.88 -> 0.87, delivery 0.86 -> 0.85) on
2026-09-01 when cairn-0033 was added: 0.851 -> 0.838 over 68 cases.
That is the SECOND time these floors have been argued down for the same
reason, and the argument was true both times. It is also exactly what a
genuine ranker regression would look like in a commit message, which is why
an aggregate floor cannot be the last line of defence. It is now the second
line. data/case-outcomes.json records the outcome of every held-out case
individually and cairn:case-guard reports the set difference, so a corpus
that grew and a ranker that broke stop being the same number.
Measured, not asserted: adding cairn-0033 broke zero existing cases -- the
whole 0.013 drop is its own first case failing, against a denominator one
larger. Dropping EXPLAINED_WEIGHT 1.0 -> 0.85 costs a comparable amount of
P@1 and DOES break an existing case (cairn-0019). Identical movement in the
average, opposite meanings, and only the per-case check can tell them apart.
RRF's k moved 60 -> 2 on 2026-09-01, and it is the first threshold in this
project chosen against more than a handful of cases. k=60 is the value from
the original RRF work, which fused TREC runs of about a thousand documents.
On a corpus of forty it inverts its own intent: 1/(60+1) against 1/(60+2) is
a 1.6% gap, so every ranker contributes nearly the same amount however
decisively it ranks, and the fusion averages noise.
Found by the agent suite, not by these numbers. On the proxy 403 stderr,
cairn-0001 led THREE of four rankers and lost the fusion by 0.16%.
Swept 1..7 and 15/30/60 on two corpora (69 and 71 held-out cases). P@1,
delivery and the agent suite are flat across the entire range; P@5 and the
proxy case are not, and the cliff sits between 3 and 4 on BOTH corpora --
a property of the ranking structure rather than of corpus size. 2 is the
paper's own ratio rescaled to these list lengths (k ~ N/17, N ~ 37) and sits
mid-plateau with two steps of headroom.
P@5 IS THIN: 0.901 against a floor of 0.90, one case from red. It was 0.913
before this change on the 69-case corpus and 0.927 after, so the fix improved
it; the two findings admitted alongside cost it again. Worth watching rather
than worth moving.
A FIFTH RANKER, `question`, added 2026-09-01 at weight 0.8. It matches the
query against the GENERATED QUESTIONS in data/expansions.json, taken at the
best single match rather than summed — question-to-question rather than
question-to-answer, which is what a searcher is actually doing. Those queries
were already being indexed, but poured into the weak text bag where one
sharply matching question is averaged away by the rest of the document.
Filling the expansion coverage gap at the same time lifted every held-out
0.863 -> 0.890. Floors left alone; see the note above about ratcheting.
delivery 0.85 -> 0.83. Five named cases given up — cairn-0005, 0007, 0019,
0030, 0032 — in exchange for field P@1 0.545 -> 1.000 and silence 0.50 ->
0.75. This is the trade cairn-0039 argues for: these queries are observation
notes written by the same author as the finding they score, and the field
suite is queries agents actually typed. Buying 45 points of the honest number
with 7 of the author-written one is the right direction, and it is a trade
rather than an improvement, which is why the cases are named.
minAnswerable, added 2026-09-01, is the number that says something about the
RANKER. P@1 over this suite is almost perfectly monotone in how much of its
own query the gold finding explains:
gold share    cases   P@1
Above 50% it is 48 of 49. The cases below are observation notes about the
BOOKKEEPING around a finding — that it ran under a sealed forecast, that it
was reclassified, that it was drafted elsewhere and handed over — and the
finding they hang off holds almost none of their vocabulary. Unwinnable by
construction, and counting them as failures understates the retriever while
making every trade against this suite look worse than it is.
The headline stays. The split is computed from the query before knowing
whether the case passed, and it is reported, not applied.
-> 0.80) by adding cairn-0040, one commit after cairn-0040 predicted exactly
this: the headline is an average over two populations, and a record about
evaluation shifts the mixture. minAnswerable — the number that measures the
RANKER — did not move at all, 0.891 before and after.
READ THESE THREE AS MIXTURE TRACKERS, NOT AS QUALITY. minAnswerable is the
quality gate. They are kept because a collapse in them would still mean
something, and dropped to just under measured because arguing them down every
time the corpus grows is the failure mode this file has already recorded.

agent._source: npm run cairn:agent-eval — real commands, real stderr
_note: silentOnUnknown counts 'returned nothing' OR 'returned only weak-labelled
matches' -- both safe; only a confident wrong answer is not.
3/3 since the failing command became evidence. Six statistical methods could
not get the third; the program name that produced the error got all three,
because it is a different KIND of evidence rather than a better weighting of
the same one.

corpus._source: npm run cairn:lint and npm run cairn:doctor

maxFalseWeak._source: fraction of CORRECT answers labelled weak
maxFalseWeak._note: If this climbs the label becomes noise and agents will ignore it.

field._source: npm run cairn:field-eval — queries agents typed mid-task, harvested from trial transcripts
_note: THE HONEST NUMBER, and it is thirty points below the held-out suite.
held-out (observation notes, author-written)   P@1 0.847
field    (typed by agents with no sight of it) P@1 0.545
Both are kept because they measure different things. The held-out suite is a
regression tripwire on a large sample; this is a small sample of what the
system is actually for. Averaging them would hide the one that matters.
minQuiet gates silence on the eight queries the corpus cannot answer. A
retriever that answers those confidently is worse than one that misses, and
nothing else in this file measures that. Two of the eight labels are
disputable and the scorer prints the band; the floor is set against the
conservative reading.
Floors are set AT the measured value, not below it. This suite is small
enough that one case is nine points, so it is a tripwire and not a target —
but it should never quietly get worse.
THE FIRST 0.545 WAS CONTAMINATED. cairn-0039 quoted these queries verbatim in
its evidence and won them on perfect coverage — a record about the eval
becoming the answer to it. De-contaminated, the real baseline was 0.455.
cairn:lint now refuses any finding or generated expansion that reproduces one.
0.455  honest baseline
0.727  + nearest-question ranker at weight 0.8
0.545  + expansions for the nine findings that had none
The last row is not a regression to hide: filling the coverage gap added nine
findings' worth of competitors, and four of the records now in the corpus are
about this project's own retrieval and measurement. The scorer prints the
decomposition (0.636 without them) rather than excluding them, because they
are real corpus members and removing them to flatter a number is rigging it.
Net against the honest baseline: +9 points on field, and the same change took
held-out P@1 from 0.849 to 0.877 and delivery from 0.863 to 0.890.
RAISED 2026-09-01: P@1 0.54 -> 0.90, quiet 0.50 -> 0.62, after reaching
11/11 and 6/8. Both floors leave room for exactly one regression. Raising a
floor on a good day is normally how it gets argued down on an ordinary one —
the exception is that this is now the metric being optimised, and an
unprotected metric is the one that quietly slides back.
1.000 ON ELEVEN QUERIES IS NOT 'SOLVED'. It is 'no longer failing on the
eleven we have'. The expansion count was chosen by measuring against these
same queries, so the guards against fitting are that both halves are perfect
INDEPENDENTLY (reachability 5/5, staleness 6/6), that 11/11 holds across a
plateau of counts rather than one lucky value, and that silence on the
unanswerable — a different population — improved at the same time.
RAISED 0.62 -> 0.75 after reaching 7/8. Seven of eight is the ceiling, not a
waypoint: the remaining query asks about half-life scoring pitfalls and is
answered by the finding about half-lives being author-supplied, which is one
of the two labels marked disputable and is arguably correct.
n GREW FROM 11 TO 22 ON 2026-09-01 and P@1 stayed 1.000. The eleven added
queries came from four traps that were never a scenario and were never tuned
against — cairn-0004, 0009, 0022, 0028 — harvested by cairn:harvest, labelled
by hand, with a forecast of 8/11 sealed and committed before scoring. The
forecast was wrong by underestimating; all eleven ranked first.
That is the first evidence here that today's tuning generalises rather than
fits. It is still ONE MODEL writing the queries, four tasks I chose, and every
new query is answerable — silence was not tested on new ground at all, and it
is the half that protects the reader. The next harvest should be built to
produce mid-task asides, which is where the unanswerable queries come from.
SILENCE RAISED 0.75 -> 0.90 after the negative half grew from 8 to 23 and
quiet reached 22/23 (0.957). The fifteen added queries came from four
debugging tasks in domains probed first and confirmed uncovered, built around
nothing in the corpus, scored before being recorded. Every one came back
quiet: 15 of 15, no confident answer to a question this corpus cannot answer.
That is the half that protects the reader and it had only ever been measured
on eight queries from scenarios the retriever was tuned against. The one
remaining CLAIMS is the disputable half-life query, unchanged.
